problem_text:
Дана разбитая на единичные клетки прямоугольная доска \(a\times b\), где \(a\) и \(b\) взаимно просты. В \(n\) клетках стоят метки; множество клеток с метками выбирается случайно и равновероятно среди всех \(n\)-элементных подмножеств клеток доски.

Из левой нижней клетки начинает двигаться фишка. За один ход она переходит в соседнюю по диагонали клетку. Изначально она идёт вверх-вправо. Если фишка должна выйти за границу доски, она отражается от стороны, как бильярдный шар, и продолжает движение по диагонали. Например, у правой границы при попытке выйти направо она просто окажется на одну клетку выше.

Фишка останавливается, когда впервые попадает в клетку с меткой.

Найдите математическое ожидание числа посещённых клеток, включая последнюю.

problem.solution:
Вместо того чтобы отражать фишку от краёв, будем каждый раз отражать саму доску. Тогда путь фишки превращается в движение по диагонали на бесконечной клетчатой плоскости.

У полученной клетчатой плоскости есть периоды \(2a\) по горизонтали и \(2b\) по вертикали, поэтому достаточно следить за координатой фишки по модулю \(2a\) и \(2b\).

Покажем, что до первого повторения фишка проходит все \(ab\) клеток исходной доски. Пусть две посещённые клетки совпали раньше, обозначим эти моменты за \(k<\ell\). Совпадение означает, что по каждой координате мы попали либо в ту же копию, либо в отражённую. Поэтому для горизонтали имеем одно из двух:
\[
k\equiv\ell\pmod{2a}
\]
или
\[
k+\ell\equiv-1\pmod{2a},
\]
и для вертикали — то же самое по модулю \(2b\).

Если в обеих координатах выбран один и тот же тип совпадения, то либо \(\ell-k\), либо \(\ell+k+1\) кратно \(2ab\). Но
\[
0<\ell-k<\ell+k+1<2ab.
\]
Если типы разные, то легко получить противоречие по чётности. Тогда за первые \(ab\) шагов мы пройдём все клетки.

Значит, фишка задаёт некоторый порядок всех клеток доски:
\[
C_1,C_2,\ldots,C_{ab}.
\]
Метки стоят в случайных \(n\) клетках, то есть в этом порядке случайно выбраны \(n\) позиций из \(1,\ldots,ab\). Фишка остановится на первой из этих позиций, осталось найти математическое ожидание минимума.

Добавим специальное число \(0\) в начало и расположим полученные \(ab+1\) чисел по кругу. Минимум выбранных чисел — это длина промежутка после \(0\) до первой выбранной точки. По симметрии средняя длина каждого из \(n+1\) промежутков одинакова, а сумма их длин равна \(ab+1\). Поэтому математическое ожидание равно
\[
\frac{ab+1}{n+1}.
\]

results.answer:
The board consists of \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns of cells, where \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), for a total of \(M=ab\) cells. Label the cells by coordinates \((r,c)\) with \(1\le r\le a\) and \(1\le c\le b\). The trajectory of the chip is modeled via the unfolding method: it corresponds to the ray \((t,t)\) for \(t\ge 0\) in the plane, with the copies of the board tiled by reflections across the boundaries. The cell visited at the \(m\)-th step along the trajectory (for \(m=0,1,\dots,ab-1\)) is the cell containing the image of the point \((m+0.5,m+0.5)\) under the folding map back to the original board. (The choice of half-integers ensures the point lies in the interior of a cell.)

The folding map for the \(x\)-coordinate (columns) is the triangle-wave function with period \(2b\): it satisfies \(\mathrm{fold}_x(s')=\mathrm{fold}_x(s)\) if and only if either \(s'=s+2kb\) or \(s'=2kb-s\) for some integer \(k\). An analogous statement holds for the \(y\)-coordinate (rows) with period \(2a\).

To show that the \(ab\) cells visited for \(m=0,\dots,ab-1\) are pairwise distinct, suppose for contradiction that two distinct indices \(m_1<m_2\) (with \(d:=m_2-m_1<ab\)) yield the same cell. Let \(s_1=m_1+0.5\) and \(s_2=m_2+0.5\). Then the folding conditions must hold simultaneously in both coordinates, yielding one of the following four combinations of relations:

- \(d=2kb\) and \(d=2ja\) for integers \(k,j\ge 1\). Then \(ja=kb\). Since \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), the minimal positive solution is \(d=2ab\), contradicting \(d<ab\).
- \(d=2kb\) and \(m_1+m_2=2ja-1\). Substituting \(m_2=m_1+d\) yields \(2m_1=2ja-d-1\). The left side is even, so the right side must be even, whence \(d\) is odd. But \(d=2kb\) is even, a contradiction.
- \(d=2ja\) and \(m_1+m_2=2kb-1\). An analogous parity argument shows that \(d\) must be odd, contradicting \(d=2ja\) even.
- \(m_1+m_2=2kb-1\) and \(m_1+m_2=2ja-1\). Then \(2kb=2ja\), and the minimal positive solution yields \(m_1+m_2=2ab-1\). But the maximal possible sum is \((ab-2)+(ab-1)=2ab-3<2ab-1\), a contradiction (and larger multiples are even bigger).

All cases are impossible. Hence the map \(m\mapsto\) cell at step \(m\) is injective. Since there are exactly \(ab\) such cells and \(ab\) cells on the board, the sequence visits every cell exactly once.

Consequently, the chip traverses a permutation \(C_1,C_2,\dots,C_{ab}\) of all cells (re-indexing from 1 for convenience) before any repetition can occur. It stops upon first reaching a marked cell, so the number \(X\) of visited cells (including the last) is the minimal index \(k\) such that \(C_k\) is marked.

The set of \(n\) marked cells is a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of the \(ab\) cells. Their positions in the fixed order \(C_1,\dots,C_{ab}\) are therefore a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of \(\{1,2,\dots,ab\}\). Thus \(X\) is the minimum value in such a random subset. For a uniform random subset of size \(n\) from \(\{1,2,\dots,M\}\) with \(M=ab\), the expectation of the minimum is \(\frac{M+1}{n+1}\). (This follows from the fact that the order statistics \(Y_1<\cdots<Y_n\) of the subset satisfy \(\mathbb{E}[Y_k]=\frac{k(M+1)}{n+1}\), or equivalently by direct summation: \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{k\ge 0}\Pr(X>k)\) with \(\Pr(X>k)=\binom{M-k}{n}/\binom{M}{n}\) for \(M-k\ge n\) and 0 otherwise, which evaluates to the stated closed form.)

Therefore the expected value is \(\frac{ab+1}{n+1}\).

(Note that this holds for \(0\le n\le ab\); when \(n=0\) the formal value \(ab+1\) corresponds to the chip traversing the entire permutation without stopping.)

Final answer: \(\dfrac{ab+1}{n+1}\)

The board consists of \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns of cells, where \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), for a total of \(M=ab\) cells. Label the cells by coordinates \((r,c)\) with \(1\le r\le a\) and \(1\le c\le b\). The trajectory of the chip is modeled via the unfolding method: it corresponds to the ray \((t,t)\) for \(t\ge 0\) in the plane, with the copies of the board tiled by reflections across the boundaries. The cell visited at the \(m\)-th step along the trajectory (for \(m=0,1,\dots,ab-1\)) is the cell containing the image of the point \((m+0.5,m+0.5)\) under the folding map back to the original board. (The choice of half-integers ensures the point lies in the interior of a cell.)

The folding map for the \(x\)-coordinate (columns) is the triangle-wave function with period \(2b\): it satisfies \(\mathrm{fold}_x(s')=\mathrm{fold}_x(s)\) if and only if either \(s'=s+2kb\) or \(s'=2kb-s\) for some integer \(k\). An analogous statement holds for the \(y\)-coordinate (rows) with period \(2a\).

To show that the \(ab\) cells visited for \(m=0,\dots,ab-1\) are pairwise distinct, suppose for contradiction that two distinct indices \(m_1<m_2\) (with \(d:=m_2-m_1<ab\)) yield the same cell. Let \(s_1=m_1+0.5\) and \(s_2=m_2+0.5\). Then the folding conditions must hold simultaneously in both coordinates, yielding one of the following four combinations of relations:

- \(d=2kb\) and \(d=2ja\) for integers \(k,j\ge 1\). Then \(ja=kb\). Since \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), the minimal positive solution is \(d=2ab\), contradicting \(d<ab\).
- \(d=2kb\) and \(m_1+m_2=2ja-1\). Substituting \(m_2=m_1+d\) yields \(2m_1=2ja-d-1\). The left side is even, so the right side must be even, whence \(d\) is odd. But \(d=2kb\) is even, a contradiction.
- \(d=2ja\) and \(m_1+m_2=2kb-1\). An analogous parity argument shows that \(d\) must be odd, contradicting \(d=2ja\) even.
- \(m_1+m_2=2kb-1\) and \(m_1+m_2=2ja-1\). Then \(2kb=2ja\), and the minimal positive solution yields \(m_1+m_2=2ab-1\). But the maximal possible sum is \((ab-2)+(ab-1)=2ab-3<2ab-1\), a contradiction (and larger multiples are even bigger).

All cases are impossible. Hence the map \(m\mapsto\) cell at step \(m\) is injective. Since there are exactly \(ab\) such cells and \(ab\) cells on the board, the sequence visits every cell exactly once.

Consequently, the chip traverses a permutation \(C_1,C_2,\dots,C_{ab}\) of all cells (re-indexing from 1 for convenience) before any repetition can occur. It stops upon first reaching a marked cell, so the number \(X\) of visited cells (including the last) is the minimal index \(k\) such that \(C_k\) is marked.

The set of \(n\) marked cells is a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of the \(ab\) cells. Their positions in the fixed order \(C_1,\dots,C_{ab}\) are therefore a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of \(\{1,2,\dots,ab\}\). Thus \(X\) is the minimum value in such a random subset. For a uniform random subset of size \(n\) from \(\{1,2,\dots,M\}\) with \(M=ab\), the expectation of the minimum is \(\frac{M+1}{n+1}\). (This follows from the fact that the order statistics \(Y_1<\cdots<Y_n\) of the subset satisfy \(\mathbb{E}[Y_k]=\frac{k(M+1)}{n+1}\), or equivalently by direct summation: \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{k\ge 0}\Pr(X>k)\) with \(\Pr(X>k)=\binom{M-k}{n}/\binom{M}{n}\) for \(M-k\ge n\) and 0 otherwise, which evaluates to the stated closed form.)

Therefore the expected value is \(\frac{ab+1}{n+1}\).

(Note that this holds for \(0\le n\le ab\); when \(n=0\) the formal value \(ab+1\) corresponds to the chip traversing the entire permutation without stopping.)

Final answer: \(\dfrac{ab+1}{n+1}\)
